title: Sesame and Lilies
author: John Ruskin
public_title: Why Does Chasing Praise Leave You Empty? | John Ruskin
hook: You check your phone constantly to see who liked your work.
source_kind: Original commentary on the retained original public-domain text; modern examples identified and limitations discussed; owner review required

source_passages.excerpt: These kings—these councillors—these statesmen and builders of kingdoms—these capitalists and men of business, who weigh the earth, and the dust of it, in a balance.
With all that they could pull out, they were not satisfied; and then, everybody wanted some of somebody else’s.
The wise religious men we have asked in vain; the wise contemplative men, in vain; the wise worldly men, in vain.
No true painter ever speaks, or ever has spoken, much of his art.
Why, you cannot even carry us up an Alp, by talking.
I know well enough what you like, and how to praise it to your better liking.
Art is neither to be achieved by effort of thinking, nor explained by accuracy of speaking.

sections.title: Section 1 links our endless chase for career status to Victo
sections.narration: You check your phone constantly to see who liked your work. A century ago, Victorian thinker John Ruskin actually found the exact same desperate hunt for social approval. He studied our obsession with prestige and wrote about it in 1865. The result? We waste our lives building empires just to impress people who do not care about us. Ruskin asked why we fight so hard for titles while ignoring true wisdom. He warned that we chase shallow praise instead of valuable knowledge. Listen to how he described these powerful figures back then: "These kings—these councillors—these statesmen and builders of kingdoms—these capitalists and men of business, who weigh the earth, and the dust of it, in a balance." They thought their wealth gave them absolute control over the world. Yet they were fundamentally empty inside. Asurion found in 2019 that people check their phones 96 times a day. We constantly measure our worth through digital applause just like those old elites.

sections.title: Section 2 connects the modern hedonic treadmill to wanting w
sections.narration: Why do we keep chasing these modern badges of honor even when they fail to make us happy? In 1978, researchers Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell showed that lottery winners return to baseline happiness levels over time. We quickly adapt to every new accomplishment. Then we look around at what others have earned. John Ruskin saw this exact same pattern destroying people in Victorian England. He wrote, "With all that they could pull out, they were not satisfied; and then, everybody wanted some of somebody else’s." Our desire for praise acts like a hedonic treadmill that never stops moving. We get a promotion or a burst of online attention. Yet we immediately start envying the person right above us. We want their status, their audience, and their praise. Chasing external applause forces you to live for someone else. You give up real purpose just to hoard approval that disappears by tomorrow morning.

sections.title: Section 3 examines why consulting worldly advice algorithms
sections.narration: Ruskin knew we naturally turn to outside experts when we feel empty inside. We search for modern algorithms and worldly advice to fix our burnout. But popular culture only offers cheap tricks that never satisfy you. Asurion found in 2019 that people check their phones 96 times a day. That's it. That is once every ten minutes, yet we still feel completely disconnected. We keep refreshing our feeds because public applause fails to heal our spirits. Ruskin saw this exact same cycle play out during the Victorian era. He warned that public opinion could never give your life real meaning. In his speech, he explained our failed search for shallow answers. "The wise religious men we have asked in vain; the wise contemplative men, in vain; the wise worldly men, in vain." External metrics will never fix an internal void. We must stop letting crowd noise dictate our true self worth.

sections.title: Section 4 contrasts modern self-promoting influencers with t
sections.narration: Modern creators spend hours shouting for attention online. They post every detail to get instant validation. But John Ruskin saw through this noisy trap long ago. He knew that deep mastery requires quiet dedication instead of constant self-promotion. As Ruskin observed, "No true painter ever speaks, or ever has spoken, much of his art." Real masters focus entirely on the work itself. They do not waste time begging for applause. You might wonder, does sharing every single goal online actually help you achieve it? In 2009, psychologist Peter Gollwitzer showed that announcing a goal publicly reduces your actual effort. Your brain experiences a premature sense of completion. True greatness is built in silence. When you stop chasing public praise, your real talent finally has room to grow.

sections.title: Section 5 reveals why endlessly talking about our goals neve
sections.narration: Ruskin knew that loud boasting accomplishes nothing. He wrote, "Why, you cannot even carry us up an Alp, by talking." We love to talk about our big ambitions. We share every project online before we even start. But talking about a mountain does not climb it. Researcher Peter Gollwitzer showed this in 2009. When you announce a goal publicly, your brain gets tricked. It feels a fake sense of victory right away. That quick burst of praise steals your drive. You feel like you won, so you stop trying. Real work requires quiet grit. You must carry the weight step by step. Stop broadcasting your every move to the world. Put your head down and do the hard labor. Let your actual progress speak for itself.

sections.title: Section 6 explains how social media algorithms manipulate yo
sections.narration: Ruskin saw this exact trap coming over a century ago. He wrote, "I know well enough what you like, and how to praise it to your better liking." That is the exact business plan of every modern algorithm. These apps do not want to enrich your mind. They study your cheap desires and feed them back to you. They flatter your worst instincts just to keep your eyes on the screen. Why does this constant digital applause feel so addictive? Research from 2019 shows people check their phones 96 times a day. That is once every ten minutes. The apps trigger tiny hits of validation to keep you hooked. They make you think you are gaining real respect. In reality, you are just feeding a machine that profits off your vanity. You trade deep human connection for worthless digital pats on the back.

sections.title: Section 7 shows how deep craft happens through quiet focus r
sections.narration: To break this cycle, you must reclaim your quiet focus. Deep work requires total silence, not a constant audience. John Ruskin believed true creation demands humble, unselfish devotion. As he wrote, "Art is neither to be achieved by effort of thinking, nor explained by accuracy of speaking." Psychology backs this up today. Researcher Peter Gollwitzer proved that publicly announcing your goals tricks your brain into feeling a false sense of completion. You lose the actual drive to finish the work. True mastery happens in the shadows, far away from public applause. Stop performing for strangers who do not truly care about your growth. Build your skill for the sake of the craft itself. So next time you reach for a quick dopamine hit, remember that silence creates lasting value. Resist the urge when you check your phone constantly to see who liked your work.
